Photograph: georgeclerk/Getty Images/iStockphoto UK news Murder inquiry opens after death of man bitten by dog in West Yorkshire Detectives say 55-year-old man arrested and appeal for anyone who witnessed altercation in Wakefield Hannah Al-Othman North of England correspondent Sun 16 Aug 2026 09.04 EDT Last modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 11.35 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Police in West Yorkshire have launched a murder investigation into the death of a man after he was bitten by a dog. Officers were dispatched to Wakefield just after 1.30pm on Saturday, after receiving reports of an altercation a short time earlier on an old trainline footpath. During the altercation a 55-year-old man was bitten by a dog. He was taken to hospital in a critical condition and died shortly after 7pm. A 55-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of murder and being the owner of a dog dangerously out of control in a public place causing injury, police said, adding that he was in custody. Police seized a dog which was understood to have been the one involved in the incident. The homicide and major inquiry team are investigating the man’s death and detectives appealed for any witnesses, including two women who stepped in to help the victim, to come forward. DCI Michael Cox said: “Sadly, a man has died and it is really important that we understand the circumstances of what has taken place. “We know that two people, one named Sophie, stopped to assist the injured man and direct officers. We would urge these two women to come forward to help us with our ongoing inquiries into this tragic incident. “The initial altercation has happened in an area used by walkers and we are urging anyone who has potentially seen or heard any part of the exchange between these two men to please make contact.” Anyone with information can contact detectives via www.westyorkshire.police.uk/livechat or by calling 101, quoting crime reference 13260465524. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cp9e.text: Image source, Getty Images By Bethany Bell Germany reporter Published 8 hours ago German intelligence believes a cache of guns found in the woods near Berlin last year was for carrying out assassinations on behalf of Russia, reports say. Germany's Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said federal prosecutors were investigating a suspect in Romania over suspicions of espionage and "the preparation of a serious act of violence threatening the state". While refusing to confirm reports of Russian links to the cache, Dobrindt said he could not rule out "the involvement of foreign powers". For months security agencies have warned that Russian intelligence services are planning assassinations in Germany, possibly targeting defence industry executives or opposition figures in exile. Image source, EPA Image caption, Alexander Dobrindt, in a photo taken earlier this month Dobrindt said that last October Germany's domestic intelligence agency became aware of a possible weapons cache in the woods on the outskirts of Berlin. Officials located the stash with the help of the Berlin State police, and found two handguns and ammunition. The German security authorities suspect the weapons and ammunition found were intended for use in attacks. Reports in German daily newspaper SÃ¼ddeutsche Zeitung and the public broadcasters NDR and WDR say the cache was to facilitate targeted killings on behalf of Moscow. Dobrindt said after the guns were rendered inoperable, the weapons cache was placed under surveillance for months but nobody was seen approaching it. "This case demonstrates that we are operating under a high threat level," Dobrindt said. The minister said prosecutors were investigating a suspect in Romania, who is being held in connection with planned parcel bomb attacks there. He said this would be taken into account when it came to a possible extradition. He described the suspect as a "low-level agent", and declined to disclose his nationality. Several similar operatives had been detained so far this year, he said, including one person from Kazakhstan. The investigation follows previous accusations of Russian attacks on German soil. In 2024, German political figures reacted angrily to a CNN report that Russia had plotted to kill the head of Germany's biggest arms company Rheinmetall, Armin Papperger. In 2021 a German court jailed Russian national Vadim Krasikov for life for a murder in a Berlin park and said it had been ordered by Moscow . Krasikov was later freed in a prisoner swap. https://dominicanrepublicpost.com/a-pain.text: Caribbean News A Painting Made For The Dominican Republic Just Got Ripped Off Its Embassy Wall For Being “Too Woke” 27 August 2026 Support us By NAN Staff Writer, NewsAmericas Now News Americas, SANTO DOMINGO, Dominican Republic, Thurs. August 27, 2026: A painting the U.S. government commissioned specifically to honor Dominican art and artists has been torn down from the American Embassy in Santo Domingo, and the State Department now wants to sell it. “Young Artists After Siamesas 1960,” by acclaimed Us-born artist Kehinde Wiley , best known for painting Barack Obama’s official presidential portrait, depicts four Dominican models against a floral backdrop. It wasn’t a generic import: Wiley spent two years studying the work of Dominican modernists Celeste Woss y Gil and Gilberto Hernández Ortega, collaborating directly with art students from Santo Domingo’s Facultad de Artes and the Altos de Chavón School of Design to create it. Taxpayers funded the commission in 2013, and the State Department itself awarded Wiley its Medal of Arts in 2015 specifically “for his longtime contributions to Art in Embassies and cultural diplomacy.” Wiley is a renowned artist who has firmly situated himself within art history’s portrait painting tradition. As a contemporary descendant of a long line of portraitists, including Reynolds, Gainsborough, Titian, Ingres, among others, Wileyengages the signs and visual rhetoric of the heroic, powerful, majestic, and the sublime in his representation of urban Black and Brown men found throughout the world. Torn down and covered in a flag FLASHBACK – Visitors view the official portraits of former president Barack Obama by artist Kehinde Wiley and former first lady Michelle Obama by Amy Sherald at The Art Institute of Chicago on June 18, 2021, in Chicago, Illinois. Chicago is the first stop of the Obama Portraits Tour, organized by the Smithsonian’s National Portrait Gallery and running from June 2021 through May 2022. Other scheduled stops on the tour include New York, Los Angeles, Atlanta, and Houston. (Photo by Scott Olson/Getty Images) Last week, embassy staff removed the painting, but not before draping it in a tarp printed with an American flag first. Erin Scavino, director of the Art in Embassies program, called it “very woke” and “aesthetically terrifying” in a podcast interview, adding, “It was by the gentleman who did Obama’s portrait.” U.S. Ambassador to the Dominican Republic Leah Campos celebrated the removal on social media with a video set to the rock anthem “We’re Not Gonna Take It,” writing that the painting represented “globalist and woke ideologies.” Neither official explained what was actually objectionable about the artwork itself. Asked directly about the painting’s content, a State Department spokeswoman instead pointed to unrelated 2023 comments Wiley had made about a different, separate painting, and to sexual assault accusations Wiley has publicly denied. “The work of an individual with such violent and racist words and depictions has no place in the America First State Department,” the spokeswoman said, confirming the department is now exploring whether it can legally sell the piece. A program built for exactly this Virginia Shore, who ran the Art in Embassies acquisitions program from 2000 to 2017 and commissioned the Wiley piece, pushed back directly. “Calling this woke is difficult for me to understand,” she said. “This is a program validated and financially backed under Bush. There is a science of building trust and empathy across borders.” The Art in Embassies program dates to the Kennedy administration in 1963, created specifically to foster cultural diplomacy through art reflecting the countries embassies serve, exactly what a two-years-in-the-making painting made with and for Dominican artists represents. There’s no precedent for the government selling an existing embassy artwork, according to Shore. A smaller Wiley painting sold at auction in 2024 for nearly $845,000. Part of a pattern The Dominican painting’s removal isn’t an isolated incident. Scavino has claimed credit for pushing out an ambassador in Bucharest, Romania, over what she called “satanic baby art,” though that departure was officially reported as a planned retirement. She also appointed a friend with no curatorial experience to run the U.S. Pavilion at the Venice Biennale, bypassing normal selection procedures, and organized a Washington exhibition this July built around nearly 70 versions of the American flag. For a piece specifically created to honor Dominican art, Dominican artists, and Dominican cultural identity, on the walls of the embassy meant to represent America to the Dominican Republic, its removal raises an obvious question: what, exactly, about honoring the Dominican Republic’s own artistic heritage was considered un-American in the first place?
